quote: Ist $f(x)$ nach $p$ in $\nu$ irreducible Faktoren zerlegbar, so ist $f(x)$ nach [-...-] jeder Potenz von $p$ in ebensoviel Faktoren zerlegbar, ausser wenn $p$ ein Teiler der Discriminante ist und diese Eigenschaft charakterisirt auch wahr- scheinlich umgekehrt die Teiler der Discriminante.
english: If f(x) is decomposable modulo p into ν irreducible factors, then f(x) is decomposable modulo every power of p into equally many factors, except when p is a divisor of the discriminant; and conversely this property probably also characterizes the divisors of the discriminant.
topic: Hilbert discusses when a polynomial f(x) splits modulo powers of a prime p in the same way as modulo p, notes that this fails when p divides the discriminant, and begins a proof using a Galois field, a prime ideal of p and the subfield attached to the group of substitutions fixing that prime ideal.

triage.modern_statement: Take a monic integer polynomial f(x) and suppose it factors modulo p into ν irreducible factors. Does f then factor into ν factors modulo every power p^k, so that the factorization lifts to the p-adic integers Z_p, whenever p does not divide disc(f)? And conversely, does this lifting property pick out exactly the primes that divide the discriminant? (Hilbert works in a Galois field with a prime ideal over p and its decomposition group, so in number-field terms this is about which primes are unramified, i.e. the primes not dividing the field discriminant.)
triage.answered_by: The direct statement is Hensel's lemma. If p does not divide disc(f), then f mod p has no repeated factors, so its factors are pairwise coprime and lift uniquely modulo every p^k and to Z_p. Kurt Hensel proved this around 1897–1904 when he created the p-adic numbers. The number-field version, linking ramified primes to the discriminant, is Dedekind's theorem (1878; the Dedekind–Kummer theorem). Hilbert's converse, as written for the discriminant of the polynomial, is false. A simple check (my own, not from a source): f = x^2 − p^2 has discriminant 4p^2, which p divides, yet f = (x−p)(x+p) splits into the same two factors modulo every p^k. The correct converse uses the field discriminant: p ramifies if and only if p divides the field discriminant (Dedekind; Hensel also gave a p-adic criterion for this).

evidence.claim: Hensel's lemma: because the lifts to each power of p fit together as p grows (an inverse limit), a root or factorization modulo p can be lifted to one over the p-adic integers.
Hensel created the p-adic numbers near the start of the 20th century.
The lemma for lifting a factorization of a univariate polynomial is originally due to Kurt Hensel.
A historical study of Hensel's work describes a p-adic criterion for when p divides the discriminant, which Hensel used to decide whether p ramifies.
The Dedekind–Kummer theorem connects how p factors in O_K with how a polynomial factors modulo p.

triage.why: The forward claim is exactly Hensel's lemma for factors that are coprime modulo p, which is now standard textbook material. Hilbert's 'probably conversely' does not hold for the polynomial discriminant: x^2 − p^2 is a counterexample, and primes that divide the polynomial's index but not the field discriminant are another source of trouble. It becomes correct in Dedekind's form, where ramified primes are exactly those dividing the field discriminant. This note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Confidence is medium because I identified the problem from the page summary and my own mathematical reasoning; the counterexample and the coprime-factors argument are mine, not taken from the sources, and no source discusses this diary entry directly.
